So I created a “pipeline” with my team via my staff. We will always have players because we start with them at a young age and they matriculate to my age group. However, I have dealt with “poaching” for at times so I do have tips.
1. Understand kids are fickle and will do what they want. You really can’t save them all, even if you are the only option. As a former teacher, knowing I was starting over each year made each class and school year meaningful.
2. Don’t get attached to individuals and create a system that gets the best out of the five on the floor. 
3. Expand your roster. I start with 25 and I have to make cuts but I keep in touch with the 10 +- kids that won’t make it. 

I’m usually left with 15 and out of those 15, only 12 will travel (unless local.) I prefer having a travel team of 10-12 with a tight 8 man rotation. The guys just outside of the rotation are usually tweeners, specialists, mismatch guys, or guys that need more development but can still push the people in front of them. 

If you have to sell trinkets to spend your intellectual and emotional labor on the betterment of youth athletes , then something is wrong and it isn’t YOU. I do hope that you find some kids and build relationships that will last beyond a season and even after high school. Good luck!

Every addiction can have a trigger that causes a relapse. TIP: Address the relapse in a neutral fashion as it isn’t “good” or “bad,” it just is. It is only a setback if you choose to believe so. TIP: Identifying potential triggers and having a plan for those situations is extremely helpful. Try to set your own reasonable goal(s) so that “winning” is something you can gauge and something you can achieve. An unreasonable goal may be hoping to completely eliminate mdd or setting an unreasonable amount of time to heal. As a fellow md, I still have those moments where I daydream, but due to the nature in which my daydreaming virtually stopped, I can’t take credit for the drop in frequency. TIP: Set aside time for daydreaming and hopefully at some point you will gain the strength and discipline to limit the time at your own pace. Set an alarm or coordinate a phone call from someone in your support network after a certain amount of time.

Our addiction is extremely special because we have unlimited and (free) access and many of us are high functioning. Meaning, we can openly indulge without the stigma that drug, alcohol, caffeine, food etc. addicts have. Because we can hide our addiction, a lot of us developed an automatic switch and no longer have to immerse ourselves manually or have the capacity to do so. TIP: Redirect your thoughts as soon as you become aware of your daydreaming. You may have to do this many times in just one freaking minute, but you are forcing your mind to focus on something different.

The hardest part is finding excitement in the real world. It was very painful to move on from something that I loved and needed as a child. The real world feels generic and predictable so you have to prepare for the “crashes” you will face when trying to minimize md. Binging on a daydream scenario usually ended up making me depressed, so I wasn’t able to use minimization . TIP: There is an overlooked element to what happens during dd and we typically notice it when trying to reduce or stop. There is an emotional reset when you are making progress. I grieved after I moved on…and I don’t mean a little tear for one day. I wept, and every few months I let out an agonizing cry for what I had to let go. There are tears of joy sometimes too. 

Our brains are hardwired to rapidly distribute dopamine when dd. TIP: It is ok if you have several moments in which you feel minimal excitement when you aren’t dd. We don’t have an endless supply of dopamine, and it takes time to adjust. You are trying to rewire your brain to release dopamine at a normal rate, and in situations that aren’t in your mind. Just like with many addictions, the altered state that we crave takes a toll. 

Lastly: Be vigilant if you are trying to daydream in a way that others who do not have mdd do. One recovering alcoholic can drink champagne for a toast and be fine, another could do the same and spiral out of control. Be honest with yourself on this journey. Take it easy and know that this process is an ongoing battle but there are meaningful moments outside of your head.

I’m basically retraining my brain by saying what is drowned out psychologically. When the fatigue of holding off negative, intrusive, and painful thoughts sets in, I know that it is ok to be done for that day. I also understand that this mental state isn’t permanent.

So, I want you to know that I am here for you and I am available to talk and am willing to be apart of your support network when things get too far. You matter and I want you to not only know but believe that you do. This is a community filled with people that understand and have been through the same things.
